newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Zaire rebels offer temporary ceasefire.
newsitem.headline: Zaire rebels offer temporary ceasefire.

text.p: Tutsi rebels in eastern Zaire on Monday offered a three-week ceasefire after a string of military successes which has turned more than a million Rwandan Hutu into refugees stranded with little food or water.
The rebels warned that combat would resume if Zaire did not agree the truce -- a tall order for the Kinshasa government which is committed to recapturing lost towns.
France proposed an international conference to examine how to restore security in eastern Zaire to allow refugees to return to their camps.
French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette told reporters the proposal was aimed at France's partners, including the United States, the European Union, the Organisation of African Unity and Canada.
Rebel leader Laurent Kabila said his fighters would begin a three-week ceasefire from 5 p.m. (1500 GMT) to allow Rwandan and Burundian Hutu refugees to return home from Zaire.

"The Alliance for Democracy following a unilateral decision will have a ceasefire to start at 5 p.m. today for three weeks," Kabila said in a telephone call to a correspondent for Voice of America radio in the Burundian capital Bujumbura.
"This is because of the disquiet of the international community, to allow the International Red Cross to evacuate the refugees who want to return to their original countries," he added.

"We hope that the unilateral ceasefire will be respected by the Zairean side. If they are against this decision, then combat will restart immediately," added Kabila, who said he was speaking from the rebel-held eastern Zairean city of Bukavu.
The refugees have so far refused to return to Rwanda, fearing punishment for the 1994 genocide of minority Tutsis in which many took part.
Tens of thousands of Hutu militiamen and former Rwandan soldiers, many of them armed, are among the refugees.
Concern over the Rwandan refugees mounted to fever pitch.

"How many pictures of massacres and of dying babies will it take before the heads of state and U.N. react?" asked the relief agency Medecins Sans Frontieres (Doctors without Borders) in a call for international military intervention.
Earlier Kabila urged relief teams to return to rebel-held eastern Zaire to care for the refugees.

"We give them security so that they can land and use the airport at Kilimba close to Uvira as well as in Goma, which is completely under our control," Kabila, who is not a Tutsi, said in an interview with the British Broadcasting Corporation (BBC).
Uvira, on the northern shore of Lake Tanganyika and south of Goma, was taken by the rebels more than a week ago.
It was not possible to confirm independently the rebel claim to have seized all of the city of Goma, where fierce fighting over the weekend forced all international aid workers to flee.
Goma was reported calm on Monday.

Peter Kessler, a spokesman for the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees (UNHCR), said the question of access to the refugees, who face the threat of death by starvation or epidemics, would be discussed on Monday in Rwanda.
He said assistant High Commissioner Sergio Vieira de Mello was due in the capital Kigali for talks with Rwanda's Tutsi-led government, which is sympathetic to the rebels.
Asked whether the United Nations would enter rebel-held territory to feed the refugees, Kessler said: "There has to be a clear mandate (from the United Nations)."
Diplomats noted that there was the precedent of northern Iraq, where the international community had ignored the central government in Baghdad and arrived with humanitarian aid.

UNHCR head Sadako Ogata said in Geneva on Sunday that "emergency lifelines" should be opened to help the refugees and displaced Zaireans alike, with corridors for the Hutus to return in safety to their homes in Rwanda and Burundi.
Reuters correspondent Christian Jennings, in the Rwandan border town of Gisenyi right next to Goma, said the border crossing was held by rebels on Monday and no fighting was heard all morning.
The crisis for Zaire has sharpened with the absence of veteran President Mobutu Sese Seko, receiving treatment for cancer in Switzerland.

Zaire accuses Tutsi-led Rwanda, which has long complained of cross-border raids by Hutu hardliners living among the refugees, of sending troops to fight alongside the rebels. Journalists saw Rwandan troops in Goma on Saturday. Rwanda denies involvement.
